lessons.title: Modules and imports
lessons.body:
# Modules and imports

Every `.py` file is a module. A folder of modules is a package. `import` runs a module's top-level code once, caches it in `sys.modules`, and gives you a name for it.

```python
import math
import json as js
from collections import Counter

print(math.pi)
print(js.dumps({"a": 1}))
print(Counter("aab"))
```

## Where Python looks

Python searches the folders in `sys.path`: the script's folder, then the standard library, then installed packages. A file named `random.py` next to your script hides the real `random`, so avoid names of standard modules.

## The main guard

```python
def main():
    print("running")

if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()
```

A module's `__name__` is `"__main__"` only when it runs as a script, so importing this file will not start `main`. Prefer `import x` over `from x import *`, so readers can see where every name came from.
lessons.task: Import from the standard library at the top of the file. Write `circle_area(r)` using `math.pi`. Write `most_common_word(words)` using `from collections import Counter`, returning the most frequent word (first seen wins a tie) or `None` for an empty list. Write `to_json(data)` returning JSON text with sorted keys.

checks.name: uses math.pi
checks.code:
import math
assert math.isclose(circle_area(2), math.pi * 4), circle_area(2)

checks.name: imports Counter by name
checks.code:
from collections import Counter as real_counter
assert globals().get("Counter") is real_counter, "use: from collections import Counter"

checks.name: most common word
checks.code:
got = most_common_word(["a", "b", "b", "c"])
assert got == "b", got

checks.name: ties and empty lists
checks.code:
got = most_common_word(["x", "y", "y", "x"])
assert got == "x", got
assert most_common_word([]) is None, most_common_word([])

checks.name: JSON with sorted keys
checks.code:
got = to_json({"b": 1, "a": [True, None]})
assert got == '{"a": [true, null], "b": 1}', got

hints: All three tools come from the standard library: `math`, `collections` and `json`. Your imports go at the top.
`Counter(words).most_common(1)` returns a list holding one `(word, count)` pair. `json.dumps` has a `sort_keys` argument.
`Counter(words).most_common(1)[0][0]` after handling the empty list, and `json.dumps(data, sort_keys=True)`.
lessons.explanation:
`most_common` orders equal counts by first appearance, so ties resolve predictably without extra code.

`import math` keeps the module name visible at the call site. `from collections import Counter` is reasonable when one name is used often and its origin is obvious.

lessons.title: Packages
lessons.body:
# Packages

A package is a folder of modules. Its `__init__.py` runs once, the first time anything from the package is imported, and the names it defines become the package's attributes. Technically a package is a module with a `__path__`: the list of folders its submodules are loaded from.

```python
import importlib
import os
import sys
from pathlib import Path

Path("shop").mkdir(exist_ok=True)
Path("shop/prices.py").write_text(
    "TAX = 0.2\n")
Path("shop/__init__.py").write_text(
    "from .prices import TAX\n"
    "__all__ = ['TAX']\n")
sys.path.insert(0, os.getcwd())
importlib.invalidate_caches()

import shop
print(shop.TAX, shop.__all__)
print(shop.prices.__name__)
print(shop.__path__)
```

## Inside a package

- `from .prices import TAX` is a relative import: `.` is this package and `..` its parent. It works only in a module imported as part of a package.
- A submodule loads only when something imports it. Here `import shop` loads `shop.prices` because `__init__.py` imports it.
- `__all__` lists the names that `from shop import *` binds. Without it, every name not starting with `_` is bound.

Keep `__init__.py` short: re-export the public names and leave the real work in submodules.
lessons.task: Write `is_package(module)`, true when the module has a `__path__`. Write `public_names(module)` returning what `from module import *` would bind: `module.__all__` as a list when it exists, otherwise the sorted names not starting with `_`. Write `submodule_names(package)` returning the sorted names of every module in the package's folders, imported or not, using `pkgutil.iter_modules`.

checks.name: packages have a __path__
checks.code:
import json
import json.decoder
assert is_package(json), "json is a package"
got = is_package(json.decoder)
assert not got, "json.decoder is a plain module"

checks.name: __all__ decides what a star import binds
checks.code:
import importlib, os, sys
from pathlib import Path
Path("kit").mkdir(exist_ok=True)
Path("kit/tools.py").write_text("def f():\n    return 1\n")
Path("kit/__init__.py").write_text("from .tools import f\nVERSION = 1\n__all__ = ['f']\n")
sys.path.insert(0, os.getcwd())
importlib.invalidate_caches()
kit = importlib.import_module("kit")
assert is_package(kit), "kit is a package"
got = public_names(kit)
assert got == ["f"], got

checks.name: without __all__, public names are bound
checks.code:
import importlib, os, sys
from pathlib import Path
Path("plain_mod.py").write_text("A = 1\n_hidden = 2\ndef go():\n    pass\n")
sys.path.insert(0, os.getcwd())
importlib.invalidate_caches()
plain_mod = importlib.import_module("plain_mod")
got = public_names(plain_mod)
assert got == ["A", "go"], got

checks.name: finds submodules nobody imported yet
checks.code:
import importlib, os, sys
from pathlib import Path
Path("box/inner").mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
for name in ["box/__init__.py", "box/a.py", "box/b.py", "box/inner/__init__.py"]:
    Path(name).write_text("")
sys.path.insert(0, os.getcwd())
importlib.invalidate_caches()
box = importlib.import_module("box")
got = submodule_names(box)
assert got == ["a", "b", "inner"], got

hints: Every package has a `__path__` attribute and plain modules do not. `__file__` will not tell them apart, because packages have one too.
`hasattr(module, "__all__")` tells you whether `__all__` exists. For the folder listing, `pkgutil.iter_modules(package.__path__)` yields objects with a `.name`.

`return hasattr(module, "__path__")`; `return list(module.__all__)` when it exists, else `sorted(n for n in vars(module) if not n.startswith("_"))`; and `sorted(m.name for m in pkgutil.iter_modules(package.__path__))`.
lessons.explanation:
`dir(package)` lists only the submodules that something has already imported, because importing a package runs `__init__.py` and nothing more. `pkgutil.iter_modules` reads the package's folders instead, so it also finds modules nobody has loaded yet.

`__path__` is the real mark of a package: it tells the import system where to look for `package.name`. `__all__` is a statement of the public interface, which is why star imports and documentation tools respect it.

lessons.title: Identity, equality and copies
lessons.body:
# Identity, equality and copies

`==` asks whether two objects have equal values. `is` asks whether two names refer to the very same object, the one `id(x)` identifies. Use `is` for `None` and other singletons, and `==` for everything else. Small ints and short strings are sometimes shared, so `is` can seem to work on them; never rely on it.

```python
import copy

a = [1, 2]
b = [1, 2]
print(a == b, a is b)  # True False

t = (a, "x")
a.append(3)
print(t)  # the list inside changed

shared = [a, a]
deep = copy.deepcopy(shared)
print(deep[0] is deep[1])  # True
```

## Mutable and immutable

Lists, dicts, sets and most objects can change in place, and every name bound to one sees the change. Numbers, strings, tuples and frozensets cannot. A tuple is only as fixed as what it holds: a tuple containing a list can still change, so it cannot be hashed.

`x += y` changes a list in place but builds a new object for a tuple or a string. A function that receives a list receives that same list, not a copy.

`copy.deepcopy` copies nested objects all the way down and keeps shared references shared, so the copy has the same shape as the original.
lessons.task: Write `unique_objects(items)` dropping repeats of the same object, by identity rather than equality, keeping the first. Write `with_item(order, item)` returning a new order dict whose `"items"` list ends with `item`, leaving `order` and the list inside it unchanged. Write `freeze(data)` returning a hashable copy of nested data: lists and tuples become tuples, sets become frozensets, and dicts become tuples of `(key, value)` pairs sorted by key, all recursively.

checks.name: unique by identity, not equality
checks.code:
a = [1]
b = [1]
got = unique_objects([a, b, a])
assert len(got) == 2, got
assert got[0] is a and got[1] is b, "keep a and b: equal, but different objects"
assert unique_objects([]) == [], unique_objects([])

checks.name: with_item returns the new order
with_item leaves the original alone
freeze goes all the way down
checks.code:
got = freeze([1, [2, [3]]])
assert got == (1, (2, (3,))), got
hash(got)

checks.name: freeze handles dicts and sets
checks.code:
got = freeze({"b": [1], "a": {2}})
assert got == (("a", frozenset({2})), ("b", (1,))), got
hash(got)

checks.name: freeze copies and keeps plain values
checks.code:
data = {"x": [1]}
freeze(data)
assert data == {"x": [1]}, data
assert freeze("text") == "text", freeze("text")
assert freeze(5) == 5, freeze(5)

hints: `==`, and so `in`, treat two equal lists as the same item. `id(obj)` is unique among living objects and works even for unhashable items such as lists.
A shallow copy of `order` still shares its `"items"` list. In `freeze`, check the container type and call `freeze` again on every element.

A `seen` set of `id(item)` values; `copy.deepcopy(order)` before appending; and in `freeze`, `tuple((k, freeze(v)) for k, v in sorted(data.items()))` for dicts, `tuple(freeze(x) for x in data)` for lists and tuples, `frozenset(...)` for sets.
lessons.explanation:
`in` and `==` compare values, so two equal lists looked like one object. Comparing `id` values, which is what `is` does, keeps distinct objects apart even when they are equal. `copy.copy(order)` copied the dict but shared its list, so `append` reached the caller's order.

Turning only the outer list into a tuple leaves the inner lists mutable, and `hash` refuses a tuple that holds a list. Freezing has to go all the way down, for the same reason `deepcopy` exists: copying one level protects only one level.

lessons.title: Bytes, str and Unicode
lessons.body:
# Bytes, str and Unicode

A `str` is a sequence of Unicode code points. A `bytes` object is a sequence of numbers from 0 to 255. Files, networks and hashes work in bytes, so text is encoded on the way out and decoded on the way in.

```python
s = "café"
b = s.encode("utf-8")
print(len(s), len(b))  # 4 5
print(b)               # b'caf\xc3\xa9'
print(b[0], list(b[3:]))
print(b.decode("utf-8"), ord("é"))
```

UTF-8 uses one byte for ASCII and up to four for other characters, so the length in characters and the length in bytes differ. Decoding with the wrong codec raises `UnicodeDecodeError` or, worse, quietly produces the wrong text. `errors="replace"` puts the marker U+FFFD in place of bad bytes.

## Equal-looking text

```python
import unicodedata

a = "café"
b = "café"
print(a == b, len(a), len(b))
nfc = unicodedata.normalize("NFC", b)
print(a == nfc)
```

The same letter can be one code point or a letter plus a combining accent. `normalize("NFC", s)` picks the composed form. For case-insensitive comparison use `s.casefold()`, a stronger `lower()` that also turns ß into ss.
lessons.task: Write `utf8_size(text)` returning how many bytes `text` takes in UTF-8. Write `safe_decode(data)` decoding UTF-8 bytes with each invalid byte replaced by U+FFFD instead of raising. Write `same_text(a, b)` telling whether two strings match after NFC normalization and case folding.

checks.name: counts bytes, not characters
checks.code:
assert utf8_size("abc") == 3, utf8_size("abc")
assert utf8_size("café") == 5, utf8_size("café")
assert utf8_size("日本") == 6, utf8_size("日本")
assert utf8_size("\U0001D11E") == 4, utf8_size("\U0001D11E")

checks.name: decodes good bytes
checks.code:
got = safe_decode(b"caf\xc3\xa9")
assert got == "café", repr(got)

checks.name: replaces bad bytes
checks.code:
got = safe_decode(b"ok\xff!")
assert got == "ok�!", repr(got)

checks.name: composed and decomposed forms match
checks.code:
assert same_text("café", "café"), "the two spellings of café should match"
assert not same_text("cafe", "café"), "a missing accent is a different word"

checks.name: ignores case, including ß
checks.code:
assert same_text("Straße", "STRASSE"), "ß case-folds to ss"
assert same_text("Hello", "hELLO"), "case should not matter"
assert not same_text("a", "b"), "different letters"

hints: `len` counts code points. Encode the text first and measure the bytes.
`bytes.decode` takes an `errors` argument. For the comparison, combine `unicodedata.normalize("NFC", s)` with `s.casefold()`.
`len(text.encode("utf-8"))`, `data.decode("utf-8", errors="replace")`, and compare `unicodedata.normalize("NFC", s.casefold())` for both strings.
lessons.explanation:
`len(text)` counts code points, so `"café"` is 4 even though it needs 5 bytes. Anything that stores or sends text, from file sizes to network limits, needs the encoded length.

`lower()` does not turn ß into ss, and plain `==` sees a precomposed é and an e followed by a combining accent as different strings. Case folding and normalizing both sides gives a key that compares the way people read text.

lessons.title: Classes
lessons.task: Write `Wallet(owner, balance=0)` with `deposit(amount)` and `withdraw(amount)`, each returning the new balance and raising `ValueError` for a non-positive amount or, for `withdraw`, too little money. Its repr is `Wallet('Ada', 10)`. Write `SavingsWallet(Wallet)` taking `rate=0.1`, with `add_interest()` adding `balance * rate`.

checks.name: deposit and withdraw
checks.code:
w = Wallet("Ada")
assert w.balance == 0, w.balance
assert w.deposit(10) == 10, w.balance
assert w.withdraw(3) == 7, w.balance

checks.name: rejects bad amounts
can withdraw everything
checks.code:
w = Wallet("Ada", 5)
assert w.withdraw(5) == 0, w.balance

checks.name: repr
checks.code: assert repr(Wallet("Ada", 10)) == "Wallet('Ada', 10)", repr(Wallet("Ada", 10))

checks.name: wallets are independent
checks.code:
a = Wallet("A")
b = Wallet("B")
a.deposit(5)
assert b.balance == 0, b.balance

checks.name: savings wallet inherits and adds interest
checks.code:
s = SavingsWallet("Bo", 100, rate=0.5)
assert isinstance(s, Wallet), type(s).__mro__
s.add_interest()
assert s.balance == 150, s.balance
assert s.deposit(50) == 200, s.balance
assert SavingsWallet("Bo").rate == 0.1, SavingsWallet("Bo").rate

hints: Store `balance` on `self` in `__init__`. Everything else reads and updates `self.balance`.
Validate first and change the balance after, so a failed call leaves it untouched. In the subclass, call `super().__init__(owner, balance)`.
`if amount > self.balance: raise ValueError("not enough money")`. For the repr: `f"Wallet({self.owner!r}, {self.balance})"`. In `add_interest`: `self.balance += self.balance * self.rate`.
lessons.explanation:
Validating before changing state means a raised error leaves the object as it was. That is the easiest invariant to keep.

`!r` in the f-string uses `repr`, which adds the quotes around the owner name. The subclass reuses parent setup through `super()` instead of repeating it, so a later change to `Wallet` reaches both classes.

lessons.title: Inheritance and super()
lessons.task: Make `Colored` and `Bordered` cooperative: each `__init__` takes keyword-only arguments, keeps its own (`color="black"`, `width=1`) and passes the rest to `super().__init__`, and each `describe` extends `super().describe()`. Then `Badge(name="ok", color="red", width=2).describe()` returns `["ok", "2px", "red"]`.

checks.name: each class works alone
checks.code:
c = Colored(name="a", color="red")
assert c.describe() == ["a", "red"], c.describe()
b = Bordered(name="b")
assert b.describe() == ["b", "1px"], b.describe()

checks.name: Badge sets every attribute
checks.code:
b = Badge(name="ok", color="red", width=2)
got = (b.name, b.color, b.width)
assert got == ("ok", "red", 2), got

checks.name: defaults still apply in a Badge
checks.code:
b = Badge(name="ok")
got = (b.color, b.width)
assert got == ("black", 1), got

checks.name: describe visits every class once
checks.code:
got = Badge(name="ok", color="red", width=2).describe()
assert got == ["ok", "2px", "red"], got

checks.name: super() reaches a class it never names

hints: `Shape.__init__(self, name)` always jumps straight to `Shape`, skipping any class that sits between them in a `Badge`'s MRO.
Give each `__init__` the form `def __init__(self, *, color="black", **kwargs)` and call `super().__init__(**kwargs)` first. Do the same for `describe`.
`Bordered.describe` returns `super().describe() + [f"{self.width}px"]` and `Colored.describe` returns `super().describe() + [self.color]`. A `Badge`'s MRO is `Badge, Colored, Bordered, Shape`.
lessons.explanation:
Naming the parent directly works in a single chain and breaks with two parents. `Colored.__init__` had no place for `width` and called `Shape.__init__` itself, so `Bordered.__init__` never ran and a `Badge` had no `width` at all.

`super()` follows the MRO of the actual object. For a `Badge` the order is `Badge`, `Colored`, `Bordered`, `Shape`, so `Colored` hands on to `Bordered` without knowing it exists. Keyword arguments let each class take what it understands and forward the rest.

lessons.title: Equality, hashing and ordering
lessons.task: Write `Version(text)` storing `text` and `parts`, the tuple of ints from a string like `"1.10.2"`. Versions compare by `parts` with all six comparison operators, work as set members and dict keys, return `NotImplemented` against other types, and repr as `Version('1.10.2')`.

checks.name: parses numbers
checks.code:
got = Version("1.10.0").parts
assert got == (1, 10, 0), got
assert repr(Version("1.4.2")) == "Version('1.4.2')", repr(Version("1.4.2"))

checks.name: equal versions
checks.code:
assert Version("1.2") == Version("1.2"), "same parts should be equal"
assert Version("1.2") != Version("1.3"), "different parts should differ"

checks.name: orders numerically
checks.code:
assert Version("1.9") < Version("1.10"), "1.9 comes before 1.10"
assert Version("2.0") >= Version("1.10"), "2.0 >= 1.10"
assert Version("1.0") <= Version("1.0"), "1.0 <= 1.0"
assert Version("3.1") > Version("3.0.9"), "3.1 > 3.0.9"
got = [v.text for v in sorted([Version("1.10"), Version("1.2"), Version("1.9")])]
assert got == ["1.2", "1.9", "1.10"], got

checks.name: works in sets and as dict keys
checks.code:
got = len({Version("1.0"), Version("1.0"), Version("2.0")})
assert got == 2, got
assert {Version("1.0"): "x"}[Version("1.0")] == "x", "equal versions should find the same key"

checks.name: other types
checks.code:
assert (Version("1.0") == "1.0") is False, "a Version never equals a str"
raised = False
try:
    Version("1.0") < 3
except TypeError:
    raised = True
assert raised, "Version < int should raise TypeError"

hints: Compare tuples of ints, not strings: `"10" < "9"` is true for strings.
Start `__eq__` and `__lt__` with `if not isinstance(other, Version): return NotImplemented`. Add `@total_ordering` for the other operators, and a `__hash__`.
`self.parts = tuple(int(p) for p in text.split("."))`, `return self.parts < other.parts` in `__lt__`, and `return hash(self.parts)` in `__hash__`.
lessons.explanation:
Comparing text sorts `"1.10"` before `"1.9"`, because strings compare character by character. Tuples of ints compare number by number, which is how versions work.

Once a class defines `__eq__`, Python sets its `__hash__` to `None`, because the inherited identity hash would break the rule that equal objects hash equally. Hashing `parts`, the same data `__eq__` compares, restores it. Returning `NotImplemented` instead of raising lets `==` with a string quietly give `False`, while `<` with a number raises `TypeError`.

lessons.title: Properties
lessons.task: Write `Temperature(celsius)` where `celsius` is a property whose setter raises `ValueError` below -273.15, including in `__init__`. Add a `fahrenheit` property with a setter that stores the matching Celsius value, and a read-only `kelvin` property.

checks.name: reads all three scales
checks.code:
import math
t = Temperature(20)
assert t.celsius == 20, t.celsius
assert math.isclose(t.fahrenheit, 68), t.fahrenheit
assert math.isclose(t.kelvin, 293.15), t.kelvin

checks.name: setting fahrenheit updates celsius
checks.code:
import math
t = Temperature(0)
t.fahrenheit = 212
assert math.isclose(t.celsius, 100), t.celsius

checks.name: celsius is checked on every assignment
checks.code:
raised = False
try:
    Temperature(-300)
except ValueError:
    raised = True
assert raised, "Temperature(-300) should raise ValueError"
t = Temperature(5)
raised = False
try:
    t.celsius = -274
except ValueError:
    raised = True
assert raised, "t.celsius = -274 should raise ValueError"
assert t.celsius == 5, t.celsius

checks.name: fahrenheit is checked too
checks.code:
t = Temperature(5)
raised = False
try:
    t.fahrenheit = -500
except ValueError:
    raised = True
assert raised, "-500 F is below absolute zero"
assert t.celsius == 5, t.celsius

checks.name: kelvin is read-only
checks.code:
t = Temperature(0)
raised = False
try:
    t.kelvin = 10
except AttributeError:
    raised = True
assert raised, "assigning to kelvin should raise AttributeError"
assert isinstance(Temperature.__dict__.get("celsius"), property), "celsius should be a property"

hints: Store the real value as `self._celsius`, and make `celsius` a property whose setter validates before storing.
The `fahrenheit` getter computes `self.celsius * 9 / 5 + 32`. Its setter converts back and assigns `self.celsius`, so the same check runs.
`@fahrenheit.setter` with `self.celsius = (value - 32) * 5 / 9`, and `kelvin` as a `@property` returning `self.celsius + 273.15`, with no setter.
lessons.explanation:
Validating only in `__init__` leaves a gap: any later `t.celsius = -500` goes straight in. With a property, every assignment, including the one in `__init__`, runs the setter.

Routing the Fahrenheit setter through `self.celsius` reuses that single check instead of copying it. Leaving `kelvin` without a setter makes it derived data that cannot drift out of step with the stored value.

lessons.title: Class and static methods
lessons.task: Write `Color(r, g, b)` that limits each channel to 0..255 with a static method `clamp(value)`, a class method `from_hex(text)` turning `"#ff8000"` into the matching color of whichever class it is called on, and a repr like `Color(255, 128, 0)` that uses the instance's own class name.

checks.name: clamp works on the class and on instances
checks.code:
assert Color.clamp(300) == 255, Color.clamp(300)
assert Color.clamp(-5) == 0, Color.clamp(-5)
assert Color(0, 0, 0).clamp(7) == 7, "clamp should also work when called on an instance"

checks.name: channels are clamped
checks.code:
c = Color(300, -1, 10)
got = (c.r, c.g, c.b)
assert got == (255, 0, 10), got

checks.name: from_hex
checks.code:
c = Color.from_hex("#ff8000")
assert (c.r, c.g, c.b) == (255, 128, 0), repr(c)
c = Color.from_hex("#0A0B0C")
assert (c.r, c.g, c.b) == (10, 11, 12), repr(c)

checks.name: subclasses get their own type
checks.code:
class Shade(Color):
    pass
s = Shade.from_hex("#000000")
assert type(s) is Shade, type(s).__name__
assert repr(s) == "Shade(0, 0, 0)", repr(s)

checks.name: repr
checks.code: assert repr(Color(1, 2, 3)) == "Color(1, 2, 3)", repr(Color(1, 2, 3))

hints: `@staticmethod` lets `clamp` be called on the class or an instance with just `value`. Use it in `__init__` as `self.clamp(r)`.
`@classmethod` gives `from_hex` the class as `cls`. Build the result with `cls(r, g, b)` so subclasses get their own type. `int("ff", 16)` reads hex.
`digits = text.removeprefix("#")`, then `int(digits[0:2], 16)` and so on, `return cls(r, g, b)`, and `type(self).__name__` in the repr.
lessons.explanation:
A function in a class body without a decorator becomes an ordinary method, so `Color(0, 0, 0).clamp(7)` passed the instance as `value` and failed. `@staticmethod` switches that off.

A static `from_hex` that calls `Color(...)` always builds a `Color`, even when called as `Shade.from_hex`. A class method receives the class it was called on, so `cls(...)` builds the right type, and `type(self).__name__` keeps the repr honest for subclasses.

lessons.title: Dataclasses
lessons.body:
# Dataclasses

`@dataclass` writes `__init__`, `__repr__` and `__eq__` from a list of annotated fields. Use it for objects that mainly hold data.

```python
from dataclasses import dataclass, field

@dataclass
class Order:
    item: str
    qty: int = 1
    notes: list[str] = field(
        default_factory=list)
```

Each `Order` gets its own `notes` list. A plain `notes: list = []` is rejected with an error, because all instances would share one list.

## Options

- `frozen=True` makes instances immutable and hashable, so they can be dict keys.
- `order=True` adds `<`, `>` and friends, comparing fields in order.
- `slots=True` uses less memory and blocks stray attributes.

## Validation

`__post_init__` runs right after the generated `__init__`:

```python
from dataclasses import dataclass

@dataclass
class Age:
    years: int

    def __post_init__(self):
        if self.years < 0:
            raise ValueError("negative")

print(Age(12))
```

import dataclasses
assert dataclasses.is_dataclass(Task), "use @dataclass"
t = Task("write")
assert (t.title, t.priority, t.tags) == ("write", 0, []), t

assert Task("a", 1) != Task("a", 2), "different fields should differ"

checks.name: tags are not shared
checks.code:

b = Task("b")
a.tags.append("x")
assert b.tags == [], b.tags

checks.name: rejects an empty title
Point is frozen
checks.code:
import dataclasses
p = Point(1, 2)
assert (p.x, p.y) == (1, 2), p
raised = False
try:
    p.x = 5
except dataclasses.FrozenInstanceError:
    raised = True
assert raised, "assigning to a frozen Point should raise"

checks.name: Point is hashable
checks.code:
assert {Point(1, 2): "a"}[Point(1, 2)] == "a", "equal points should find the same key"

hints: Import `dataclass` and `field` from `dataclasses`, and put the annotated fields directly in the class body.
A list default needs `field(default_factory=list)`. Validation goes in `__post_init__`, and `@dataclass(frozen=True)` handles `Point`.
`tags: list[str] = field(default_factory=list)`, then `def __post_init__(self): if not self.title: raise ValueError("title is required")`.
lessons.explanation:
`default_factory` runs once per instance, so tags are never shared. Dataclasses refuse a bare mutable default because it would be a bug in nearly every case.

Freezing a dataclass with the default `eq=True` also generates `__hash__`. That is what lets `Point` work as a dict key. Hash and equality must agree, and frozen fields cannot change, so they always will.

lessons.title: Slots
lessons.body:
# Slots

Each instance normally keeps its attributes in a dict, `obj.__dict__`. That is flexible, and it costs memory for every object. Listing the attribute names in `__slots__` gives instances fixed storage instead.

```python
class Plain:
    def __init__(self, x):
        self.x = x

class Slim:
    __slots__ = ("x",)

    def __init__(self, x):
        self.x = x

p, s = Plain(1), Slim(1)
p.typo = 2  # silently accepted
print(hasattr(s, "__dict__"))
try:
    s.typo = 2
except AttributeError as e:
    print(e)
```

## What changes

- Assigning a name that is not in `__slots__` raises `AttributeError`, which catches misspellings such as `self.raduis`.
- Instances are smaller and attribute access is a little faster. It matters when you create many thousands of objects.
- A subclass without its own `__slots__` gets a `__dict__` back. Give each subclass `__slots__` listing only its new names.
- A slotted name cannot also have a class-level default. Set defaults in `__init__`.

`@dataclass(slots=True)` writes `__slots__` for you.
lessons.task: Give `Vector(x, y)` `__slots__` so instances have no `__dict__` and reject unknown attributes. Make `Vector3(Vector)`, which adds `z` defaulting to 0, keep the same restriction by listing only its new name in its own `__slots__`.

checks.name: Vector has no instance dict
checks.code:
v = Vector(1, 2)
assert (v.x, v.y) == (1, 2), (v.x, v.y)
assert not hasattr(v, "__dict__"), "add __slots__ to Vector"

checks.name: unknown attributes are rejected
checks.code:
v = Vector(1, 2)
raised = False
try:
    v.z = 3
except AttributeError:
    raised = True
assert raised, "v.z = 3 should raise AttributeError"

checks.name: slotted attributes can still change
checks.code:
v = Vector(1, 2)
v.x = 5
assert v.x == 5, v.x

checks.name: Vector3 keeps the restriction
checks.code:
w = Vector3(1, 2, 3)
assert (w.x, w.y, w.z) == (1, 2, 3), (w.x, w.y, w.z)
assert Vector3(1, 2).z == 0, Vector3(1, 2).z
assert not hasattr(w, "__dict__"), "give Vector3 its own __slots__"

checks.name: Vector3 lists only z
checks.code:
slots = Vector3.__dict__.get("__slots__", ())
names = [slots] if isinstance(slots, str) else list(slots)
assert names == ["z"], names

hints: `__slots__` is a class attribute: a tuple of the attribute names instances may have.
A subclass needs its own `__slots__` too, or Python quietly gives its instances a `__dict__` again. List only the names the subclass adds.
`__slots__ = ("x", "y")` in `Vector` and `__slots__ = ("z",)` in `Vector3`. Mind the comma: `("z")` is just a string.
lessons.explanation:
Without `__slots__`, `v.z = 3` quietly adds an entry to the instance's dict, so a typo becomes a silent bug. With slots there is no dict to add to.

Slots are per class. `Vector3` inherits the storage for `x` and `y`, and repeating those names would waste space, so it lists only `z`. If a subclass leaves out `__slots__` entirely, its instances get a `__dict__` again, and both the saving and the protection are gone.

lessons.title: Enums
lessons.body:
# Enums

An enum is a fixed set of named constants. Each member has a `name` and a `value`, and a member is never mistaken for a plain string or number.

```python
from enum import Enum, auto

class Status(Enum):
    DRAFT = auto()
    LIVE = auto()
    ARCHIVED = auto()

s = Status.LIVE
print(s, s.name, s.value)
print(Status["DRAFT"], Status(3))
print([m.name for m in Status])
print(s is Status.LIVE, s == 2)
```

- `Status["DRAFT"]` looks a member up by name and `Status(3)` by value. Unknown input raises `KeyError` or `ValueError`.
- Each member exists once, so `is` and `==` agree. Iteration follows definition order.
- A member never equals its raw value: `Status.LIVE == 2` is false. `StrEnum` and `IntEnum` members do equal their values, which helps when they travel through JSON or a database.
- An enum can have methods, which receive the member as `self`.
- Any name assigned in the class body becomes a member, so keep helper tables inside methods.
lessons.task: Write an enum `Light` with `RED`, `YELLOW` and `GREEN`, valued `"red"`, `"yellow"` and `"green"`, and a method `next()` that follows the cycle red, green, yellow, red. Write `parse_light(text)` returning the member whose value matches `text` ignoring case and surrounding spaces, or `None`.
lessons.starter:
from enum import Enum


class Light(Enum):
    RED = "red"
    YELLOW = "yellow"
    GREEN = "green"

    def next(self):
        members = list(Light)
        i = members.index(self)
        return members[(i + 1) % len(members)]


def parse_light(text):
    return Light[text]

checks.name: members and values
checks.code:
import enum
assert issubclass(Light, enum.Enum), "Light should be an Enum"
got = [(m.name, m.value) for m in Light]
assert got == [("RED", "red"), ("YELLOW", "yellow"), ("GREEN", "green")], got

checks.name: cycles red, green, yellow
checks.code:
assert Light.RED.next() is Light.GREEN, Light.RED.next()
assert Light.GREEN.next() is Light.YELLOW, Light.GREEN.next()
assert Light.YELLOW.next() is Light.RED, Light.YELLOW.next()

checks.name: parses values in any case
checks.code:
assert parse_light(" Red ") is Light.RED, parse_light(" Red ")
assert parse_light("GREEN") is Light.GREEN, parse_light("GREEN")
assert parse_light("yellow") is Light.YELLOW, parse_light("yellow")

checks.name: unknown text gives None
checks.code:
assert parse_light("blue") is None, parse_light("blue")
assert parse_light("") is None, parse_light("")

hints: `Light("red")` looks a member up by its value, and raises `ValueError` when there is none.
Clean the text with `strip()` and `lower()` before the lookup, and catch the `ValueError`. For `next`, a dict from each member to the following one is clearer than index arithmetic.

In `next`: `return {Light.RED: Light.GREEN, Light.GREEN: Light.YELLOW, Light.YELLOW: Light.RED}[self]`. In `parse_light`: `try: return Light(text.strip().lower())` and `except ValueError: return None`.
lessons.explanation:
`Light[text]` looks up names, not values, and raises for anything unexpected. `Light(value)` is the value lookup, and catching its `ValueError` turns bad input into `None`.

The cycle is not the definition order, so stepping through `list(Light)` gives the wrong next light. Spelling the transitions out makes the rule visible. The table lives inside the method because a dict assigned in the class body would become a member itself, and the members do not exist yet while the body runs.

lessons.title: Protocols and duck typing
lessons.body:
# Protocols and duck typing

Python does not ask what class an object is. It asks whether the object has the attribute you are about to use. That is duck typing: if it has `.read()`, it can be read.

```python
def shout(thing):
    return thing.text().upper()
```

Any object with a `text` method works, and no shared base class is needed.

## Writing the contract down

`typing.Protocol` names the shape you expect, so type checkers can verify it. Classes do not inherit from it.

```python
from typing import Protocol
from typing import runtime_checkable

@runtime_checkable
class HasText(Protocol):
    def text(self) -> str: ...

class Note:
    def text(self):
        return "hi"

isinstance(Note(), HasText)  # True
```

`runtime_checkable` allows `isinstance`, but it only checks that the method name exists. It does not look at parameters or return types.
lessons.task: Write a runtime-checkable protocol `Renderer` with `render(self) -> str`. Write classes `Text(value)` rendering the value and `Bold(value)` rendering `**value**`, neither inheriting from `Renderer`. Write `render_all(items)` joining the rendered items with newlines.

checks.name: renders each class
checks.code:
assert Text("a").render() == "a", Text("a").render()
assert Bold("a").render() == "**a**", Bold("a").render()

checks.name: joins with newlines
checks.code:
got = render_all([Text("a"), Bold("b")])
assert got == "a\n**b**", repr(got)
assert render_all([]) == "", render_all([])

checks.name: accepts any object with render
matches the protocol
checks.code:
assert isinstance(Text("a"), Renderer), "Text should match Renderer"
assert isinstance(Bold("a"), Renderer), "Bold should match Renderer"
assert not isinstance(3, Renderer), "an int has no render method"

checks.name: no inheritance needed
checks.code:
assert Renderer not in Text.__mro__, "Text should not inherit from Renderer"
assert Renderer not in Bold.__mro__, "Bold should not inherit from Renderer"

hints: A protocol is a class that inherits `Protocol`, with method bodies of `...`. Add `@runtime_checkable` above it.
`Text` and `Bold` each gain a `render` method. `render_all` only needs to call `.render()`, without checking types.
`class Renderer(Protocol):` with `def render(self) -> str: ...`, and `return "\n".join(i.render() for i in items)`.
lessons.explanation:
`render_all` never names a class, so it accepts anything with a `render` method, including classes written later.

A protocol adds a checkable contract without forcing a shared base class. Use one when you want tools to catch a missing method before the code runs. `isinstance` against a protocol only confirms the name exists, so it is not a full proof.

lessons.task: Make `Storage` an abstract base class with abstract `load(key)` and `save(key, value)`, keeping its concrete `update(key, fn)`, which saves `fn(old value)` and returns it. `MemoryStorage(Storage)` keeps values in a dict, and its `load` raises `KeyError` for a missing key.

checks.name: Storage cannot be created
an incomplete subclass cannot be created
exactly load and save are abstract
checks.code:
got = sorted(getattr(Storage, "__abstractmethods__", ()))
assert got == ["load", "save"], got

checks.name: memory storage works
checks.code:
s = MemoryStorage()
s.save("a", 1)
assert s.load("a") == 1, s.load("a")
assert isinstance(s, Storage), "MemoryStorage should subclass Storage"
raised = False
try:
    s.load("missing")
except KeyError:
    raised = True
assert raised, "loading a missing key should raise KeyError"

checks.name: update is shared
checks.code:
s = MemoryStorage()
s.save("n", 2)
got = s.update("n", lambda v: v * 10)
assert got == 20, got
assert s.load("n") == 20, s.load("n")

hints: Inherit from `ABC` and put `@abstractmethod` above each method that subclasses must write.
An abstract method's body can be just `...`. `update` stays an ordinary method: it calls `self.load` and `self.save`, whatever the subclass made them.
`from abc import ABC, abstractmethod`, `class Storage(ABC):`, then `@abstractmethod` above `def load(self, key): ...` and above `def save(self, key, value): ...`.
lessons.explanation:
Raising `NotImplementedError` only fails when someone finally calls the missing method, which may be deep inside a running program. `@abstractmethod` moves the failure to the moment an incomplete object is created, with an error naming what is missing.

`update` is written once, in terms of `load` and `save`, and every storage gets it. That split, where the base class owns the steps and subclasses fill in the details, is the main reason to write an ABC rather than a protocol.

Change `Notifier` to receive a sender object in `__init__`, anything with `send(text)`, instead of inheriting from `EmailSender`.

assert got == "Item(name='pen', price=2)", got

checks.name: the repr mixin fits any class
equality from the mixin

assert Item("pen", 2) == Item("pen", 2), "same attributes should be equal"
assert Item("pen", 2) != Item("pen", 3), "different prices should differ"
assert (Item("pen", 2) == "pen") is False, "an Item never equals a str"

checks.name: the notifier uses the sender it is given
the notifier holds a sender instead of being one
checks.code: assert EmailSender not in Notifier.__mro__, "Notifier should not inherit from EmailSender"

hints: `vars(self)` is the dict of an instance's attributes, in the order they were set.
In `__eq__`, return `NotImplemented` unless `type(other) is type(self)`, then compare `vars(self) == vars(other)`. `Notifier.__init__` just stores the sender.
`fields = ", ".join(f"{k}={v!r}" for k, v in vars(self).items())` and `return f"{type(self).__name__}({fields})"`. In `notify`, call `self.sender.send(f"{user}: {text}")`.

Inheriting from `EmailSender` welded `Notifier` to one way of sending. A test could not swap in a fake without patching, and adding text messages would mean another subclass. Holding the sender as an attribute makes it a choice made by whoever builds the `Notifier`.

The mixins read only `vars(self)` and `type(self)`, so they fit any class and need no setup. That is what keeps mixins safe: small, stateless, one job each.

p = Person("Ada", 36)
assert (p.name, p.age) == ("Ada", 36), (p.name, p.age)

try:
    Person("Ada", "36")
except TypeError:

assert raised, "Person('Ada', '36') should raise TypeError"
p = Person("Ada", 36)
raised = False

    p.age = 3.5

b = Person("B", 2)
assert (a.name, a.age) == ("A", 1), (a.name, a.age)

assert got == {"name": "Ada", "age": 1}, got

assert Person.age.kind is int, Person.age.kind

class Item:
    price = Typed(float)
i = Item()
i.price = 2.5

raised = False

hints: Storing the value on the descriptor, as `self.value`, shares it between every instance, because there is one descriptor per class attribute.
Add `__set_name__(self, owner, name)` to learn the attribute name, then read and write `obj.__dict__[self.name]`.
In `__get__`: `if obj is None: return self`, then `return obj.__dict__[self.name]`. In `__set__`: raise `TypeError` unless `isinstance(value, self.kind)`, then `obj.__dict__[self.name] = value`.
lessons.explanation:
A descriptor lives on the class, so one `Typed` object serves `age` for every `Person`. Keeping the value on `self` meant the last assignment won for everyone. The per-instance home for data is the instance's own `__dict__`.

Because `Typed` defines `__set__`, Python consults it before the instance dict on every lookup, so no assignment can skip the check. `__set_name__` saves repeating the name by hand, as in `age = Typed(int, "age")`.

lessons.title: Class hooks and metaclasses
lessons.task: Give `Command` an `__init_subclass__` that takes a keyword `name` and registers each subclass in `Command.registry`, raising `TypeError` if the subclass has no `run` method or the name is already taken. `dispatch(name)` creates the registered command and returns its `run()` result, raising `KeyError` for unknown names.

checks.name: subclasses register themselves
dispatch runs the command
unknown names raise KeyError
run is required
names are unique

hints: `__init_subclass__(cls, name, **kwargs)` runs as each subclass is created, and raising there stops the class from being created at all.
Check before registering: `getattr(cls, "run", None)` must be callable, and `name` must not already be a key of `Command.registry`.
`if not callable(getattr(cls, "run", None)): raise TypeError(...)`, then `if name in Command.registry: raise TypeError(...)`, and only then `Command.registry[name] = cls`.
lessons.explanation:
Validating in `__init_subclass__` turns a broken plugin into an error at the line that defines it, rather than a crash the first time someone dispatches to it. Checking the name stops a later class from silently replacing an earlier one.

Every subclass shares the single `registry` dict defined on `Command`. A metaclass could do the same job, but this hook needs no new type and combines freely with other base classes.

lessons.title: Iterators and generators
lessons.body:
# Iterators and generators

An iterable is anything `for` can walk. `iter(x)` gets an iterator from it, and `next(it)` returns one item at a time, raising `StopIteration` at the end. An iterator is used up once.

```python
it = iter([1, 2])
next(it)  # 1
next(it)  # 2
# next(it) would raise StopIteration
```

A class joins in by defining `__iter__`. If `__iter__` builds a fresh iterator each time, the object can be looped over repeatedly.

## Generators

A function containing `yield` returns a generator, which is an iterator that pauses at each `yield`. Values are made on demand, so sequences can be huge or endless.

```python
def evens():
    n = 0
    while True:
        yield n
        n += 2

def both(a, b):
    yield from a
    yield from b
```

`yield from` hands over to another iterable, which is ideal for recursive walks.
lessons.task: Write a class `Countdown(start)` whose instances can be looped over more than once, producing `start` down to 1. Write a generator function `flatten(items)` yielding every non-list value from arbitrarily nested lists.

checks.code:
assert list(Countdown(3)) == [3, 2, 1], list(Countdown(3))
assert list(Countdown(0)) == [], list(Countdown(0))

checks.name: can be looped twice
checks.code:
c = Countdown(2)
assert list(c) == [2, 1], "first loop"
assert list(c) == [2, 1], "second loop should start again"

checks.name: follows the iterator protocol
checks.code:
it = iter(Countdown(1))
assert next(it) == 1, "first value"
raised = False
try:
    next(it)
except StopIteration:
    raised = True
assert raised, "an exhausted iterator should raise StopIteration"

checks.name: flattens any depth
checks.code:
got = list(flatten([1, [2, [3, [4]]], 5]))
assert got == [1, 2, 3, 4, 5], got
assert list(flatten([[], [[]]])) == [], list(flatten([[], [[]]]))

checks.name: strings stay whole
checks.code:
got = list(flatten(["ab", ["cd"]]))
assert got == ["ab", "cd"], got

checks.name: flatten is a lazy generator
checks.code:
import inspect
assert inspect.isgeneratorfunction(flatten), "flatten should use yield"
assert next(flatten([1, [2]])) == 1, "first value"

hints: If `__iter__` contains `yield`, every call to it gets a fresh generator with its own position.
In `flatten`, check `isinstance(item, list)`. A list needs another call to `flatten`, and anything else is yielded as it is.
`def __iter__(self):` with a local `n = self.start` and `while n > 0: yield n; n -= 1`. Then `yield from flatten(item)` for lists and `yield item` otherwise.
lessons.explanation:
Counting in a local variable inside `__iter__` keeps the position out of the object, so two loops over one `Countdown` cannot interfere.

`yield from flatten(item)` passes along everything the inner call produces. A generator holds one frame per nesting level, so memory use follows the depth rather than the number of items.

lessons.title: Sending into generators
lessons.body:
# Sending into generators

`yield` is an expression. `gen.send(value)` resumes a paused generator and makes the waiting `yield` evaluate to `value`, so data can flow in as well as out.

```python
def averager():
    total = count = 0
    average = None
    while True:
        value = yield average
        total += value
        count += 1
        average = total / count

avg = averager()
next(avg)  # run to the first yield
print(avg.send(10), avg.send(20))
```

A new generator has not reached a `yield` yet, so start it with `next(gen)`, which is the same as `gen.send(None)`. `gen.close()` raises `GeneratorExit` at the paused `yield` so cleanup code runs.

## yield from

`yield from inner` passes along more than values. It forwards `send` calls to `inner`, and it evaluates to whatever `inner` returns. A generator's `return x` stops it, and `x` travels in `StopIteration.value`.

```python
def inner():
    n = yield "send me a number"
    return n * 2

def outer():
    result = yield from inner()
    yield f"doubled: {result}"

g = outer()
print(next(g))
print(g.send(21))
```
lessons.task: Write a generator `running_max()` that yields the largest number sent to it so far, and `None` before the first. Write a generator `with_result(gen)` that passes on everything `gen` yields, forwards sent values to it, and then yields `gen`'s return value.

checks.name: starts with None
checks.code:
g = running_max()
got = next(g)
assert got is None, got

checks.name: tracks the maximum
checks.code:
g = running_max()
next(g)
got = [g.send(v) for v in [3, 1, 7, 7, 2]]
assert got == [3, 3, 7, 7, 7], got

checks.name: negative numbers
checks.code:
g = running_max()
next(g)
got = [g.send(v) for v in [-5, -9, -1]]
assert got == [-5, -5, -1], got

checks.name: passes items on, then the result
checks.code:
def numbers():
    yield 1
    yield 2
    return "done"
got = list(with_result(numbers()))
assert got == [1, 2, "done"], got

checks.name: forwards sent values
checks.code:
def echo():
    word = yield "ready"
    return word.upper()
w = with_result(echo())
assert next(w) == "ready", "first value"
got = w.send("hi")
assert got == "HI", got

hints: Inside the loop, `value = yield best` both hands out the current maximum and receives the next number.
Start `best` at `None`, not 0, or negative numbers break. For `with_result`, a `for` loop can neither forward `send` nor see the return value.
`if best is None or value > best: best = value`, and `result = yield from gen` followed by `yield result`.
lessons.explanation:
`for item in gen` drives `gen` with `next`, so a value sent to the outer generator never reaches the inner one, and the return value is lost inside the `StopIteration` that the loop swallows. `yield from` is full delegation: values out, sends in, and the return value back.

Starting the maximum at 0 would report 0 for a stream of negative numbers. `None` says that there is no answer yet, and the first value always replaces it.

lessons.title: The itertools module
lessons.body:
# The itertools module

`itertools` builds lazy iterators that combine like pipes. Nothing is computed until something loops over the result.

```python
from itertools import (
    accumulate, batched, chain,
    groupby, islice, pairwise)

print(list(chain([1, 2], [3])))
print(list(accumulate([1, 2, 3])))
print(list(pairwise("abc")))
print(list(batched(range(5), 2)))
print(list(islice("abcdef", 1, 4)))
for key, grp in groupby("aabccc"):
    print(key, len(list(grp)))
```

- `chain` joins iterables, and `islice` slices any iterator, even an endless one such as `count()`.
- `accumulate` yields running totals, or running results of any two-argument function, such as `max`.
- `pairwise` yields neighbouring pairs, and `batched` yields tuples of n items with a shorter last one.
- `groupby` groups only consecutive items with equal keys. Sort by the same key first if you want one group per key.
- `product`, `permutations` and `combinations` replace nested loops over choices.

These functions accept any iterable and never need `len` or indexing, so they also work on generators and files.
lessons.task: Using `itertools`, write `runs(text)` returning `(char, count)` pairs for each run of repeated characters, `increases(nums)` counting the neighbouring pairs where the second number is larger, `peaks(nums)` returning the running maximum as a list, and `pairings(names)` returning every unordered pair as a list of tuples in input order. Each must accept any iterable.

checks.name: runs of characters
checks.code:
got = runs("aabccc")
assert got == [("a", 2), ("b", 1), ("c", 3)], got
got = runs("abab")
assert got == [("a", 1), ("b", 1), ("a", 1), ("b", 1)], got
assert runs("") == [], runs("")

checks.name: counts increases
checks.code:
assert increases([1, 3, 2, 5, 6]) == 3, increases([1, 3, 2, 5, 6])
assert increases([4]) == 0, increases([4])
assert increases([]) == 0, increases([])

checks.name: running maximum
checks.code:
got = peaks([3, 1, 4, 1, 5])
assert got == [3, 3, 4, 4, 5], got
assert peaks([]) == [], peaks([])

checks.name: unordered pairs
checks.code:
got = pairings(["a", "b", "c"])
assert got == [("a", "b"), ("a", "c"), ("b", "c")], got
assert pairings(["a"]) == [], pairings(["a"])

checks.name: accepts any iterable
checks.code:
assert runs(iter("aab")) == [("a", 2), ("b", 1)], "runs of an iterator"
assert increases(x for x in [1, 2, 3]) == 2, "increases of a generator"
assert peaks(x for x in [2, 1, 3]) == [2, 2, 3], "peaks of a generator"
assert pairings(iter("xy")) == [("x", "y")], "pairings of an iterator"

hints: Each function has a matching tool: `groupby`, `pairwise`, `accumulate` and `combinations`.
`groupby(text)` yields `(key, group)` with the group as an iterator, so count it with `len(list(group))`. `accumulate` takes a function as its second argument, and `max` is one.
`[(ch, len(list(g))) for ch, g in groupby(text)]`, `sum(b > a for a, b in pairwise(nums))`, `list(accumulate(nums, max))` and `list(combinations(names, 2))`.
lessons.explanation:
The index-based versions need `len` and `nums[i]`, which generators do not have, and `text.count` counts every occurrence rather than each run. The itertools versions walk the input once, in order, so they work for any iterable.

`sum(b > a ...)` adds booleans, which count as 0 and 1. `combinations` keeps input order and never pairs an item with itself, which is exactly what an unordered pair means.

lessons.title: Comprehensions and the walrus
lessons.body:
# Comprehensions and the walrus

A comprehension inside another builds a list of lists. Two `for` clauses in one comprehension flatten instead.

```python
grid = [[1, 2, 3], [4, 5, 6]]
flat = [x for row in grid for x in row]
cols = [[row[i] for row in grid]
        for i in range(3)]
print(flat)
print(cols)

squares = (x * x for x in range(4))
print(sum(squares), sum(squares))
print({len(w): w for w in ["ab", "cd"]})
```

- A generator expression is lazy and runs once. The second `sum` finds it already empty, and a function that loops over its argument twice gets the same surprise.
- In a dict comprehension a repeated key keeps the last value.
- The loop variable stays inside the comprehension. In a class body, a comprehension cannot see the class's own names, except in its first `for`.

## The walrus operator

`:=` assigns a name and returns the value in one expression. It saves computing something twice, as in `while (line := f.readline()):`. In a comprehension the name binds in the surrounding scope.

```python
import re

words = ["a1", "b", "c22"]
nums = [int(m[0]) for w in words
        if (m := re.search(r"\d+", w))]
print(nums)
```
lessons.task: Write `transpose(matrix)` returning the columns of a list of equal-length rows as lists, using a comprehension inside a comprehension (`[]` for an empty matrix). Write `spread(values)` returning the largest minus the smallest value of any iterable, including a generator. Write `valid_numbers(items)` returning, as one comprehension, the results of the given `to_int` that are not `None`, calling `to_int` once per item.

checks.name: transpose builds rows
checks.code:
got = transpose([[1, 2, 3], [4, 5, 6]])
assert got == [[1, 4], [2, 5], [3, 6]], got
assert transpose([[7]]) == [[7]], transpose([[7]])
assert transpose([]) == [], transpose([])

checks.name: spread of a list
checks.code:
assert spread([3, 9, 4]) == 6, spread([3, 9, 4])
assert spread([5]) == 0, spread([5])

checks.name: spread of a generator
checks.code:
got = spread(x * 2 for x in [1, 5, 3])
assert got == 8, got

checks.name: keeps valid numbers, zero included
checks.code:
got = valid_numbers(["1", "x", " 7 ", "-3", "0"])
assert got == [1, 7, -3, 0], got

checks.name: calls to_int once per item

hints: For `transpose`, the outer comprehension makes one row per column index, and the inner one collects that column from every row.
A generator can be read only once, so `max` and then `min` over it cannot both work: make a list first. In `valid_numbers`, `(n := to_int(s))` stores the result and hands it to the test.
`[[row[i] for row in matrix] for i in range(len(matrix[0]))]`, `values = list(values)`, and `[n for s in items if (n := to_int(s)) is not None]`.
lessons.explanation:
Two `for` clauses in a single comprehension produce one flat list. To get rows, the inner loop must be a comprehension of its own, one per column. `[list(col) for col in zip(*matrix)]` is a shorter spelling of the same idea.

`max(values)` used up the generator, so `min` saw nothing and raised `ValueError`. Calling `to_int(s)` in both the filter and the result does the work twice, and `if to_int(s)` also throws away 0. Put a one-shot iterable in a list when you need two passes, and let the walrus keep a value you need twice.

lessons.title: The collections module
lessons.body:
# The collections module

You have met `Counter`. The rest of `collections` holds more containers for jobs that plain lists and dicts do awkwardly.

```python
from collections import (
    Counter, defaultdict, deque, namedtuple)

stock = Counter(apple=3, pear=1)
sold = Counter(apple=1, pear=2)
print(stock - sold, stock + sold)

spent = defaultdict(int)
orders = [("ann", 5), ("bo", 2), ("ann", 1)]
for name, amount in orders:
    spent[name] += amount
print(dict(spent))

recent = deque("abcde", maxlen=3)
recent.appendleft("z")
print(recent)

Point = namedtuple("Point", "x y")
p = Point(1, 2)
print(p.x, p._replace(y=5), p._asdict())
```

- Counters add and subtract, and the result drops any count that falls to zero or below, which suits stock and shopping lists.
- `defaultdict` calls its factory for a missing key: `int` gives 0 for totals, `list` an empty group, `set` an empty set.
- `deque` adds and removes at both ends in constant time, where `list.pop(0)` shifts every item. With `maxlen`, items fall off the far end.
- `namedtuple` is a tuple with field names. `_replace` returns a changed copy and `_asdict` a dict.
lessons.task: Write `shortfall(needed, have)` returning a dict of how many of each item in the list `needed` are still missing after using the list `have`, with no zero entries. Write `totals(pairs)` summing the amounts of `(name, amount)` pairs per name into a plain dict. Write `tail(items, n)` returning the last `n` items of any iterable as a list. Define `Card = namedtuple("Card", "rank suit")`.

checks.name: shortfall
checks.code:
got = shortfall(["egg", "egg", "milk", "flour"], ["egg", "flour", "flour"])
assert got == {"egg": 1, "milk": 1}, got
assert shortfall(["a"], ["a", "b"]) == {}, shortfall(["a"], ["a", "b"])

checks.name: totals per name
checks.code:
got = totals([("ann", 5), ("bo", 2), ("ann", 1)])
assert got == {"ann": 6, "bo": 2}, got
assert type(got) is dict, f"return a plain dict, not {type(got).__name__}"
assert totals([]) == {}, totals([])

checks.name: tail of any iterable
checks.code:
got = tail(iter(range(10)), 3)
assert got == [7, 8, 9], got
assert tail([1], 3) == [1], tail([1], 3)
assert tail([1, 2], 0) == [], tail([1, 2], 0)

checks.name: Card is a namedtuple
checks.code:
c = Card("Q", "H")
assert (c.rank, c.suit) == ("Q", "H"), c
assert c == ("Q", "H"), c
assert Card._fields == ("rank", "suit"), Card._fields
assert c._replace(rank="K") == ("K", "H"), c._replace(rank="K")

hints: `Counter(a) - Counter(b)` keeps only positive counts. `defaultdict(int)` starts every new key at 0, so `+=` just works.
A `deque` with `maxlen=n` keeps only the last `n` items it is given, and it accepts any iterable.
`dict(Counter(needed) - Counter(have))`, `sums[name] += amount` then `return dict(sums)`, `list(deque(items, maxlen=n))`, and `Card = namedtuple("Card", "rank suit")`.
lessons.explanation:
Counting with `list.count` inside a loop is slow and keeps zero and negative entries. Counter subtraction does the bookkeeping and drops what is no longer needed. Slicing with `items[-n:]` fails on iterators, and with `n` of 0 it returns everything, because `-0` is just 0.

`defaultdict(int)` removes the first-time branch, the one the starter got wrong by assigning instead of adding. Returning `dict(sums)` hands back a plain dict, so a caller's lookup of a missing name raises instead of quietly adding a zero.

lessons.title: Context managers
lessons.body:
# Context managers

`with` guarantees cleanup, whichever way a block ends. An object supports it by defining `__enter__` and `__exit__`.

```python
class Timer:
    def __enter__(self):
        return self

    def __exit__(self, kind, err, tb):
        print("done")
        return False  # do not swallow
```

`__exit__` receives details of any exception. A true return value suppresses it, so usually return `False`.

## The short form

`contextlib.contextmanager` turns a generator into a context manager. Code before `yield` is the setup. Code after it is the cleanup.

```python
from contextlib import contextmanager

@contextmanager
def tag(out, name):
    out.append(f"<{name}>")
    try:
        yield
    finally:
        out.append(f"</{name}>")
```

The `try`/`finally` matters. An exception inside the `with` block is raised at the `yield`, so without `finally` your cleanup would be skipped.
lessons.task: Write a context manager `temporary_setting(settings, key, value)` that sets `settings[key] = value` for the block, then restores the old value, or removes the key if it did not exist before. It must clean up after an exception and let the exception propagate.

checks.name: sets the value inside the block
restores the old value
checks.code:
s = {"debug": False}
with temporary_setting(s, "debug", True):
    pass
assert s == {"debug": False}, s

checks.name: removes a key that was absent
checks.code:
s = {}
with temporary_setting(s, "debug", True):
    assert s == {"debug": True}, s
assert s == {}, s

checks.name: a stored None still counts as present
checks.code:
s = {"mode": None}
with temporary_setting(s, "mode", "fast"):
    pass
assert s == {"mode": None}, s

checks.name: cleans up after an exception
nests correctly
checks.code:
s = {"n": 1}
with temporary_setting(s, "n", 2):
    with temporary_setting(s, "n", 3):
        assert s["n"] == 3, s
    assert s["n"] == 2, s
assert s["n"] == 1, s

hints: Before changing anything, record what is there now. You need to know whether the key existed and what its value was.
`None` could be a real stored value, so `key in settings` is the reliable test. Wrap the `yield` in `try`/`finally`.
`had_key = key in settings`, `old = settings.get(key)`, set the value, then `try: yield`, and `finally:` restore `old` if `had_key`, otherwise `del settings[key]`.
lessons.explanation:
An exception raised in the `with` block appears at the `yield`, so `finally` is what guarantees restoration. No `except` means the exception keeps travelling to the caller.

Testing `key in settings` separately from reading the value keeps "missing" distinct from "stored as `None`".

Write `validate(user)` that collects `KeyError("name")` when `"name"` is missing and `ValueError("age")` when `"age"` is missing or not a non-negative int, raises them together as `ExceptionGroup("invalid user", errors)`, and returns `True` when there are none.

checks.name: a valid port
checks.code: assert load_port({"port": "8080"}) == 8080, load_port({"port": "8080"})

checks.name: a missing port is chained
a bad number is chained
a valid user
checks.code: assert validate({"name": "Ada", "age": 36}) is True, "a valid user should return True"

checks.name: collects every problem
one problem is still a group

hints: `raise ConfigError("bad port") from err` needs the caught exception bound, as in `except (KeyError, ValueError) as err:`.
In `validate`, append exceptions to a list instead of raising the first one, then raise once at the end if the list is not empty.
`errors = []`, then `errors.append(KeyError("name"))` and `errors.append(ValueError("age"))` as needed, `if errors: raise ExceptionGroup("invalid user", errors)`, and `return True`.

Without `from`, the original error is only the `__context__`, and the traceback reads as if a second bug broke the handler. `from err` states that the `ConfigError` happened because of `err`, and code can inspect `__cause__` for the detail.

Raising at the first problem makes a user fix one field, submit, and meet the next. Collecting them into an `ExceptionGroup` reports everything at once, and callers can still handle each kind separately with `except*`.

lessons.title: Pattern matching
lessons.body:
# Pattern matching

`match` tries each `case` from top to bottom and runs the first one that fits. A pattern can test shape and type and pull out parts in the same step.

```python
def describe(cmd):
    match cmd:
        case ["go", direction]:
            return f"going {direction}"
        case ["take", *items] if items:
            return f"taking {len(items)}"
        case {"say": str(text)}:
            return f"saying {text}"
        case int() | float() as n:
            return f"number {n}"
        case _:
            return "unknown"

print(describe(["go", "north"]))
print(describe(["take", "a", "b"]))
print(describe({"say": "hi", "to": "x"}))
print(describe(3.5), describe("go"))
```

- A sequence pattern checks the length, and `*rest` collects the remainder. Strings never match sequence patterns.
- A mapping pattern checks only the keys it names, so extra keys are fine.
- `str(text)` checks the type and binds the value. `Point(x=0, y=y)` matches the attributes of an object.
- `|` tries alternatives, `if` adds a guard, and `as` names the whole match.
- A bare name always matches and binds. To compare with a constant, use a literal or a dotted name such as `Color.RED`.
- `case _:` catches everything else.
lessons.task: Write `evaluate(expr, env)` for small expression trees: an int or float is itself, `("neg", x)` is minus `x`, `("add", a, b)` and `("mul", a, b)` combine their evaluated parts, and `{"var": name}` is `env[name]`. Anything else raises `ValueError`.
lessons.solution:
def evaluate(expr, env):
    match expr:
        case int() | float():
            return expr
        case ("neg", x):
            return -evaluate(x, env)
        case ("add", a, b):
            return evaluate(a, env) + evaluate(b, env)
        case ("mul", a, b):
            return evaluate(a, env) * evaluate(b, env)
        case {"var": str(name)}:
            return env[name]
        case _:
            raise ValueError(f"bad expression: {expr!r}")

checks.name: numbers are themselves
checks.code:
assert evaluate(3, {}) == 3, evaluate(3, {})
assert evaluate(2.5, {}) == 2.5, evaluate(2.5, {})

checks.name: operators nest
checks.code:
got = evaluate(("add", 1, ("mul", 2, 3)), {})
assert got == 7, got
got = evaluate(("neg", ("add", 1, 1)), {})
assert got == -2, got

checks.name: variables come from env
checks.code:
got = evaluate({"var": "x"}, {"x": 10})
assert got == 10, got
got = evaluate(("mul", {"var": "x"}, 2), {"x": 3})
assert got == 6, got

checks.name: anything else raises ValueError

hints: Put the number case first, `case int() | float():`, then one tuple pattern per operator, such as `case ("add", a, b):`.
A mapping pattern, `case {"var": str(name)}:`, matches the variable form. Each operator case calls `evaluate` on its parts and passes `env` along.
Finish with `case _: raise ValueError(...)`. Negation is `case ("neg", x): return -evaluate(x, env)`.
lessons.explanation:
Indexing with `expr[0]` assumes the shape before checking it, so a short tuple raised `IndexError` and a dict raised `KeyError`. Each `case` checks the length and the tag together, and anything that fits no pattern falls through to one clear error.

The patterns read like the data they accept, so adding an operator means adding one case. A sequence pattern written with parentheses still matches lists, so `["add", 1, 2]` works too.

lessons.title: Decorators
lessons.task: Write a decorator `count_calls` that stores how many times the function ran in a `.calls` attribute, starting at 0. Write a decorator factory `retry(times)` that calls the function up to `times` times in total, returning the first success and re-raising the last exception if all fail. Both keep the function's name.

checks.name: counts calls
checks.code:
@count_calls
def add(a, b=0):
    return a + b
assert add.calls == 0, add.calls
assert add(1, b=2) == 3, "should pass arguments through"
add(1)
assert add.calls == 2, add.calls

checks.name: keeps the name
counters are separate
retries until success
gives up and re-raises
does not retry after success
checks.code:
attempts = []
@retry(5)
def fine():
    attempts.append(1)
    return "ok"
assert fine() == "ok", "return value"
assert len(attempts) == 1, attempts

hints: Functions are objects, so you can set `wrapper.calls = 0` before returning `wrapper`, and add to it inside.
`retry` has three layers: `retry(times)`, `decorator(fn)`, `wrapper(*args, **kwargs)`. The wrapper loops, and `return` inside `try` stops on the first success.
`for attempt in range(times):`, `try: return fn(*args, **kwargs)`, `except Exception:` and `if attempt == times - 1: raise`.
lessons.explanation:
Storing the count on the wrapper gives each decorated function its own counter, reachable from outside.

In `retry`, a bare `raise` inside `except` re-raises the current exception with its original traceback. Catching `Exception` leaves `KeyboardInterrupt` and `SystemExit` alone, so a stop request is never retried.

lessons.title: Functions that return functions
lessons.body:
# Functions that return functions

A function defined inside another can read the outer function's variables. When the inner function is returned, it keeps those variables alive. That pairing is a closure.

```python
def make_adder(n):
    def add(x):
        return x + n
    return add

add_two = make_adder(2)
add_two(3)  # 5
```

Each call to `make_adder` creates a new `n`, so closures from separate calls do not interfere.

## Changing a captured variable

Reading works automatically. Assigning would make a new local variable, so declare the name with `nonlocal` first:

```python
def counter():
    count = 0
    def tick():
        nonlocal count
        count += 1
        return count
    return tick
```

Closures give you small pieces of private state without a class. Reach for a class when you need several methods or want other code to inspect that state.
lessons.task: Write `running_total()` returning a function `add(n)`. Each call adds `n` to a total kept inside the closure and returns the new total. Separate calls to `running_total()` keep separate totals.
lessons.solution:
def running_total():
    total = 0

    def add(n):
        nonlocal total
        total += n
        return total

    return add

checks.name: adds up
checks.code:
add = running_total()
assert add(5) == 5, "first call"
assert add(3) == 8, "second call"
assert add(-2) == 6, "third call"

checks.name: adding zero keeps the total
checks.code:
add = running_total()
add(4)
assert add(0) == 4, "adding 0"

checks.name: totals are independent
checks.code:
a = running_total()
b = running_total()
a(10)
assert b(1) == 1, "b should not see a's total"
assert a(1) == 11, "a should keep its own total"

checks.name: state lives in the closure
checks.code:
add = running_total()
add(1)
assert add.__closure__, "add should capture total from running_total"

hints: The total has to be created inside `running_total`, so each call gets its own.
Assigning to `total` inside `add` makes Python treat it as local, which raises `UnboundLocalError`. One keyword fixes that.
Inside `running_total`: `total = 0`, then `def add(n):` with `nonlocal total`, `total += n`, `return total`. Finally `return add`.
lessons.explanation:
Each call to `running_total` runs its body once, creating a new `total` and a new `add` bound to it. The function object carries a reference to that variable in `__closure__`, which is why the value survives after `running_total` returns.

`nonlocal` tells Python that the assignment targets the enclosing variable. A module-level total would be shared by every counter.

hints: `partial(int, base=2)` is a new callable, with no `def` needed. `reduce` takes an optional third argument, the starting value.
Put `@lru_cache(maxsize=None)` above `grid_paths`. `@singledispatch` marks the fallback, and `@describe.register` above a function with an annotated parameter adds one case per type.
`reduce(operator.mul, nums, 1)`, then `@describe.register` above `def describe_int(value: int): return f"int {value}"`, and the same for `str` with `f"text {value!r}"`.
lessons.explanation:
Without a start value, `reduce` has nothing to return for an empty list and raises `TypeError`. With 1, the identity for multiplication, the empty product is 1, as in mathematics.

The uncached `grid_paths` recomputes the same smaller grids again and again, so its running time grows exponentially. With `lru_cache` each `(rows, cols)` pair is worked out once. `singledispatch` keeps each type's rule in its own function, so supporting another type means registering one more function rather than editing a branch.

lessons.title: Typing
lessons.body:
# Typing

Annotations describe what a function expects. Python does not enforce them at runtime. Tools such as type checkers and editors read them, and so do people.

```python
def lengths(
    words: list[str],
) -> dict[str, int]:
    return {w: len(w) for w in words}
```

- `list[str]`, `dict[str, int]` and `tuple[int, int]` describe contents.
- `int | None` means either one.
- `type UserId = int` creates a named alias.

## Generic functions

A type parameter links an input type to an output type:

```python
def last[T](items: list[T]) -> T:
    return items[-1]
```

Now a checker knows that `last(["a"])` is a `str`.

## Lazy annotations

Since Python 3.14, annotations are evaluated only when something asks for them, so a class can name itself in its own methods without quotes. `typing.get_type_hints(fn)` returns the evaluated annotations.
lessons.task: Add exact annotations: `word_lengths(words: list[str]) -> dict[str, int]`, and make `first_or_none` generic with a type parameter `T`, taking `items: list[T]` and returning `T | None`. Define the alias `type Scores = dict[str, int]`. Fix `first_or_none` so that it returns `None` for an empty list.

hints: Start with the annotation on `word_lengths`, which is written out in the task. Then handle the empty case of `first_or_none`.
A type parameter goes in square brackets after the function name, as in `def f[T](...)`. The alias uses the `type` statement.
`def first_or_none[T](items: list[T]) -> T | None:` with `return items[0] if items else None`, and `type Scores = dict[str, int]`.
lessons.explanation:
Annotations do not change how the code runs, which is why the empty-list bug needed a real fix. They do let a checker warn callers that the result might be `None`.

The type parameter ties the element type to the return type. `items[0] if items else None` tests whether the list is empty rather than whether its first value is falsy, so `[0]` still returns `0`.

lessons.title: Generic classes
lessons.body:
# Generic classes

The typing lesson made functions generic. Classes can take type parameters too, so a container promises that what comes out has the type of what went in.

```python
class Stack[T]:
    def __init__(self) -> None:
        self._items: list[T] = []

    def push(self, item: T) -> None:
        self._items.append(item)

    def pop(self) -> T:
        return self._items.pop()

s = Stack[int]()
s.push(3)
print(s.pop(), Stack.__type_params__)
```

`Stack[int]` tells a type checker that this stack holds ints, so `s.push("x")` is flagged before the code runs. At runtime nothing is checked.

## Bounds and the older spelling

`[T: Hashable]` limits `T` to subtypes of a type, and `[T: (int, str)]` to exactly those types. Code written before Python 3.12 declares type variables with `TypeVar` and inherits from `Generic`:

```python
from typing import Generic, TypeVar

N = TypeVar("N", bound=float)

class Box(Generic[N]):
    def __init__(self, item: N) -> None:
        self.item = item

print(Box(2.5).item, N.__bound__)
```
lessons.task: Write a generic class `Queue[T]` with `put(item: T) -> None`, `get() -> T` returning items first in, first out (raising `IndexError` when empty), and `__len__`. Then write `Labelled` in the older style: `L = TypeVar("L")` and `class Labelled(Generic[L])` whose `__init__(self, label: str, value: L)` stores both.

checks.name: Queue takes a type parameter
checks.code:
params = getattr(Queue, "__type_params__", ())
assert len(params) == 1, "write class Queue[T]:"

checks.name: first in, first out
checks.code:
q = Queue[int]()
q.put(1)
q.put(2)
q.put(3)
got = q.get()
assert got == 1, got
assert len(q) == 2, len(q)

checks.name: an empty queue raises IndexError
checks.code:
q = Queue()
raised = False
try:
    q.get()
except IndexError:
    raised = True
assert raised, "get() on an empty queue should raise IndexError"

checks.name: methods are annotated with T
checks.code:
import typing
T = Queue.__type_params__[0]
got = typing.get_type_hints(Queue.put)
assert got == {"item": T, "return": type(None)}, got
got = typing.get_type_hints(Queue.get)
assert got == {"return": T}, got

checks.name: Labelled uses TypeVar and Generic
checks.code:
import typing
assert isinstance(L, typing.TypeVar), "define L = TypeVar('L')"
assert Labelled.__parameters__ == (L,), Labelled.__parameters__
item = Labelled("size", 3)
assert (item.label, item.value) == ("size", 3), (item.label, item.value)
hints = typing.get_type_hints(Labelled.__init__)
hints.pop("return", None)
assert hints == {"label": str, "value": L}, hints

hints: Write the type parameter after the class name, `class Queue[T]:`, and use `T` in the method annotations.
`collections.deque` has `append` and `popleft`, so the oldest item comes out first. The older style needs `L = TypeVar("L")` and `class Labelled(Generic[L]):`.
`def put(self, item: T) -> None:` appends, `def get(self) -> T:` returns `self._items.popleft()`, and `Labelled.__init__(self, label: str, value: L)` stores both values.
lessons.explanation:
`list.pop()` takes from the end, so the plain class behaved as a stack. A queue takes from the front, and `deque.popleft` does that in constant time, raising `IndexError` when empty, just as the task asks.

The type parameter changes nothing at runtime, but it lets a checker know that a `Queue[str]` returns strings from `get`. `TypeVar` with `Generic` is the same idea in the older syntax, which you will meet in a lot of existing code.
